title: A field in wartime (Jeremiah 32:6–15)
hookLine: with the enemy at the gates, Jeremiah buys land: houses will be bought here again

cards: A real estate agent calls during a war. The enemy army is camped around your city. Siege ramps are going up against the walls.
Food is running out. And the agent says: there's a field for sale, just outside town. Actually, it's behind enemy lines right now.
Interested? It sounds like a joke. Jeremiah said yes.
He was under arrest at the time, held in the guard's courtyard of the king's palace, for saying out loud that Babylon would win. And his cousin came to see him with exactly that offer.

teach.b: It's the tenth year of King Zedekiah. The Babylonian army surrounds Jerusalem.

teach.h: THE RIGHT TO REDEEM IS YOURS.
teach.b: Jeremiah's cousin Hanameel comes and says: buy my field at Anathoth, our home village; the right to redeem it is yours.
In Israel's law, when family land was about to be lost, a close relative had the right, and the duty, to buy it back so it stayed in the family. God had told Jeremiah this visit was coming.
So Jeremiah does it, and does it properly.

teach.h: SEVENTEEN SHEKELS, A DEED, A JAR.
teach.b: He weighs out seventeen shekels of silver.
He signs the deed and calls witnesses. He makes two copies, one sealed and one open, and hands them to his scribe, Baruch, to put in a clay jar so they'll last a long time. Why the jar?
Because he isn't buying for this year. He's buying for after.
And he says why, in the King James Bible: "For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land."
This is the prophet who has warned for years that the city will fall. He hasn't changed his message. But he puts his money on the far side of the fall.
Then he prays, and admits it seems absurd: the city is being handed to the Chaldeans, and you told me to buy a field.

He begins: "Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee." Hope, here, isn't a feeling. It's a signed deed in a clay jar.

how: Christians often turn to Jeremiah 32 in times of crisis as a picture of hope that acts, and preachers have used it in wartime, in economic downturns and when churches build or plant in struggling neighborhoods.

games.q: you're Jeremiah, under arrest, with the enemy at the walls. your cousin offers to sell you the family field. what do you do?
o: refuse: the land is about to be lost anyway.
buy it, properly, and seal the deed in a clay jar.
promise to buy it after the war.
games.why: he buys it, with witnesses and a sealed deed: "houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land."

practice: Think of something in your world that feels besieged, your health, your town, a relationship, the news, and don't pretend it's fine; Jeremiah didn't.
Then ask what small thing you could put on the far side of it, a tree to plant, a garden bed for next spring, a letter to your future self, and picture yourself signing the deed.
If you pray, you can offer that hope to God, the way Jeremiah did.

wordCard.voice: Anathoth. Jeremiah's home village, where his cousin's field became a sealed deed bought under siege, a bet on the far side of the fall.

carryVoice: Your line: houses will be bought again. Hope, signed and sealed. Day four hundred seventy-seven, done.
